title: Crimes in New Jersey
fullText: Number one, Richard Francis Codingham. He was a computer operator. Every morning he put on a collared shirt, drove to work, managed databases at a Blue Cross Blue Shield office in Tene, New Jersey, and came home in the evenings to a house in the suburbs where his wife and three children lived. He coached little league. He attended office birthday parties. He had a pleasant enough reputation among colleagues, and beginning sometime around 1967, he was also methodically killing women. That gap between the image and what it concealed is not incidental to the story of Richard Francis Cotttingham. It is the story. Because for 13 years across New Jersey and New York, a man with no criminal profile, no obvious instability, and no apparent disruption to his domestic routine committed a series of murders. so calculated, so methodically concealed, and so extensive that investigators did not even fully understand what they were dealing with until after his arrest in 1980, and the full scope of what Cotttingham had done would not be known for another four decades beyond that. Cotttingham was born on November 25th, 1946 in the Bronx. His family relocated to Dumont, New Jersey when he was still a toddler and later to River Veil in Bergen County, a quiet northern New Jersey township of clean streets and backyard fences. By his own later account, Cotttingham developed a fixation on bondage as a teenager, a fixation that he described not as something disturbing, but as a fascination. He graduated from Pasak Valley High School in Hillsdale, New Jersey in 1964. His yearbook listed him as a member of the cross country and track teams. There was nothing to read into it. After graduation, he began working in the mail room at Metropolitan Life Insurance Company in Manhattan, where his father held a position as a vice president. He took computer courses, transferred to Blue Cross Blue Shield in 1966, and eventually became a mainframe computer operator. That career path, unremarkable as it seemed, gave Cotttingham something critically useful, a double life built around routine, predictability and the appearance of stability. He was at work every day. He was accounted for. No one looked past the surface. He married in 1970 and had three children. By 1978, his wife had filed for divorce, citing abandonment and mental cruelty. She withdrew the petition when he was arrested in 1980, then finalized the divorce after his conviction in 1981. The earliest murders Codingham has now been connected to reach back to 1967. That year, 17-year-old Maryanne Delisala disappeared after finishing her shift at a shopright in Hackinac. Her body was found 3 months later in the Payic River, strangled. Police concluded she had been killed elsewhere. In October of that same year, Nancy Vogel, a 29-year-old married mother of two whom Cotttingham knew, was found bound in her automobile in Ridgefield Park. She had been taken 3 days earlier, ostensibly on her way to play bingo with friends at a local church. She had been strangled in a field in Monil. Investigators at the time had no reason to connect either woman's death to the mildmannered computer operator in River Veil. The murders were separate cases in separate jurisdictions. They would remain unsolved for decades. This is a consistent feature of how Cotttingham operated. He did not favor a single location, a single victim type, or a single method that would generate a recognizable pattern. He moved between jurisdictions. He drugged women before transporting them across state lines using motel along the New Jersey Turnpike corridor as what investigators would eventually come to understand were his staging grounds. He approached women in bars at parking lots on street corners. He offered drinks, false promises of safety, the ordinary language of a man who did not seem dangerous. The danger only became apparent after the drugs had already taken hold. What he did after that is part of the court record. Cotttingham would bind his victims with handcuffs, gag them with adhesive tape, and subject them to extended periods of torture. He collected trophy items, jewelry, personal effects, which he stored in a locked room in the basement of his home in Loi, New Jersey. When investigators eventually searched that room and the trunk of his car following his 1980 arrest, they found property they were able to trace to multiple victims. He had kept these items for years, organized, filed away as though they were files in one of his databases. In December 1979, firefighters responding to a reported blaze at the Travelin motor in near Time Square discovered two female bodies in room 417. The room had been rented under the alias Carl Wilson. Both women had been tortured, and their killer had removed their heads and hands before setting fire to the bodies. An act investigators understood immediately was not impulse, but deliberate concealment of identity. One of the women was eventually identified as Deei Gdardi, a 22-year-old Iranian immigrant. The other has never been identified, listed only as Manhattan Jane Doe. In 2009, nearly three decades after the murders, Cottingham admitted in a prison interview that he severed the heads and hands specifically because he knew Gdarti and feared being recognized. This level of post-crime reasoning, calm, practical, directed entirely toward his own continued freedom, is what distinguished Cottingham from killers driven purely by impulse or chaos. He was deliberate. After each killing, he went back to work. He sat through meetings. He drove home to his family. In May 1980, an 18-year-old woman named Leslie Anne Odell flagged down a car near Lexington Avenue in Manhattan. The man who stopped was Richard Cottingham. He drove her to the Quality Inn in Hasbrook Heights, New Jersey. Inside the room, he drew a knife, snapped handcuffs onto her wrists, and told her she had to endure what the other girls had endured. Odell managed to reach beneath the bed for what she believed was a real firearm he had threatened her with. When it failed to fire, she screamed. Motel employees heard her. Police arrived. Cotttingham was arrested in the hallway carrying a leather gag, slave collars, a switchblade, replica pistols, and a stockpile of prescription sedatives. At the time of his arrest, the Bergen County Prosecutor's Office had no idea how extensive his crimes were. They charged him with what they could prove. Over two New Jersey trials in 1981 and 1982 and a third trial in New York in 1984, Cotttingham was convicted of multiple murders, sexual assaults, and related offenses. He received multiple life sentences, but investigators, particularly a Bergen County detective named Robert Anzelotti, never believed those convictions represented the full picture. Anelotti began reviewing cold cases from the 1960s and 1970s. In 2000, he started interviewing Cotttingham in prison from 2003 onwards. Visits that stretched across years, building slowly into something that began to resemble confession. In 2010, Cottingham pleaded guilty to the 1967 murder of Nancy Vogle. In 2014, he confessed to the murders of three teenage girls. Confessions made under a nonprosecution agreement whose details were kept from the public for several years to keep him talking. In 2021, he admitted to the 1974 double murder of two 16 and 17year-old girls from North Bergen who had been hitchhiking toward a shopping mall in Paramis. They were found bound together in Woodland in Montval, face down, both raped, both strangled. In 2022, DNA evidence connected him to the 1968 murder of a 23-year-old Long Island dance teacher, Diane Cusk, which authorities described as among the oldest criminal cases in the country to be solved through direct DNA evidence. That same year, he admitted to five further Long Island murders from the early 1970s. Keep that accumulation in mind because the timeline of what Cotttingham confessed to was still expanding well after he had entered his 70s, still imprisoned at Southwood State Prison in Bridgetton, New Jersey. He began killing in a state he never left. He killed for over a decade and was never identified. When he was finally caught, it was not due to investigative breakthrough. It was because a woman screamed loudly enough in a New Jersey motel hallway. Investigators have confirmed at least 18 to 19 killings with direct evidence or judicial acknowledgement. Cotttingham himself has claimed as many as 100. The truth lies somewhere in that range, most of it still buried in cold case files across Bergen County and beyond. What is certain is that a man who sat in a New Jersey office every day operating mainframes and tracking insurance data had a locked basement room in which he stored the possessions of dead women. At the time of this script's writing, Richard Francis Cotttingham remains incarcerated. He is in his late 70s. He is still confessing. Number two, Howard Barton UNRA. There is a detail from the morning of September 6th, 1949 that tends to get lost in the broader account of what happened on River Road in Camden. Before Howard Enra left his house, before he loaded the magazine of his Luger pistol, before he killed 13 people in 12 minutes, he sat down at the kitchen table and ate breakfast. His mother had made it. Cereal, fried eggs, and milk. He sat across from her, said nothing, and stared at her with an expression she would later describe as frightening. Then he stood abruptly, ran back into his bedroom, threatened her with a large wrench, and drove her out of the house. She ran to a neighbor. She fainted. He finished preparing his weapon, and walked outside. That breakfast, the ordinariness of it, the cereal and eggs, the mother setting the table, and what followed immediately after is the specific texture of the Howard Unrew case. It was not the work of a man who was visibly, obviously unraveling. The neighbors on River Road in East Camden had noticed changes in Unrew over the years since the war. He was sullen, paranoid, increasingly isolated. He had converted his bedroom into what one journalist described as a shrine to weaponry and war. He practiced marksmanship in the family basement almost daily. He kept a running list of grievances, neighborhood sllights, both real and imagined, each one annotated with the abbreviation DNDR, do not delay retaliation. By the summer of 1949, that list ran to nearly 200 entries. But no single neighbor had connected all of those threads into a single alarming picture. He was the odd veteran who stayed in his room. The religious one who read the Bible, the quiet one who kept to himself. Howard Barton Unrew was born on January 21st, 1921 in East Camden, New Jersey. He was the eldest of two brothers born to Samuel and Freda Unrew, a middleclass Lutheran family. As a child and teenager, he was bright but deeply withdrawn. His classmates at Woodro Wilson High School, where he graduated in January 1939, remembered him primarily for his intelligence and his distance from other people. He graduated with above average grades and the nickname How, short for Howard, the Quiet One. He had been drafted into the United States Army in 1942. Unra's military service was by any conventional measure exemplary. He was a sharpshooter and later a tank gunner. He served across Europe in campaigns including the Battle of the Bulge and the Western Allied Invasion of Germany. He was awarded the European Theater of Operations Medal and the Good Conduct Medal. He was valued by the men he served alongside. While other soldiers spent their off hours in bars or chasing women, Enra cleaned his rifle, wrote letters home to his mother, and recorded in a meticulous diary the location, date, and hour of every enemy soldier he killed, adding when possible a physical description of the body. That diary habit is worth a pause, not because it was inherently pathological. Soldiers have kept journals throughout history, but because of what it suggested about the way Unrew processed violence, he cataloged it. He organized it. He was not repulsed by it or troubled by it. He documented it the way a bookkeeper documents accounts receivable. He came back from the war in November 1945 with his medals and a marketkedly different personality. Those who had known him before recognized the change immediately. His brother and father both noted it. He was sullen. He was suspicious. He regarded other people with something close to contempt. He abandoned his earlier plans to study pharmacy. He worked briefly as a sheet metal worker, then dropped that, too. By the late 1940s, he was largely unemployed, supported by his mother's wages from a factory job, spending most of his time alone. The feud that appears most prominently in his list of grievances centered on a family named Cohen, specifically on Maurice Cohen, a pharmacist who operated a drugstore next to the Unrew family home. The dispute had multiple origins. Unrew's habit of cutting through the Cohen's backyard as a shortcut. Unrew's mother asking him to turn his wireless down. One of the Cohen children playing a bugle too loudly. minor irritants, the kind that arise between any two households sharing a common boundary. To Maurice Cohen, they were probably forgotten within a week. To Howard Unra, they were evidence of persecution. Each one logged and assigned a retaliation notation. In September 1949, Unra installed a large security gate in his backyard to block his neighbors access. On the night of September 5, he went to a Philadelphia cinema, one he frequented for reasons he would later describe to investigators, and returned home around 3:00 in the morning. The gate was gone. Someone had stolen it overnight. He lay on his bed, still dressed, staring at the ceiling. He did not sleep. He waited for morning. At 9:17 a.m. on September 6th, 1949, Howard Unra stepped off his back porch through the gap where his gate had been and walked onto River Road. He was dressed in a brown worsted suit. In his jacket pocket, a loaded Luger, a spare eight- round magazine, a hunting knife, and a tear gas pen with six shells. He would inform investigators later that he had also brought the knife because he had initially intended to behead the Cohen family. He did not do so. There was no time. What followed across the next 12 minutes has been documented precisely because multiple witnesses survived, because journalists arrived quickly, and because UNRA himself gave an extensive and methodical account under police interrogation. He shot the shoe maker. He shot the barber and a six-year-old sitting in a novelty carousel horse. He shot the pharmacist. He shot the pharmacist wife inside a storage cupboard. He shot the pharmacist's mother as she reached for a telephone. He shot the pharmacist himself as he tried to escape across porch roof. First in the back, then through the back of the head with a careful second aim. He shot a driver who had stopped to help. He shot a woman and her elderly mother in a car waiting at a stoplight. He shot the woman's 10-year-old son who died the following morning at the hospital. He walked to a Taylor's shop, found the tor absent, and shot the tor's wife of two months in the kitchen as she sank to her knees and begged for her life. He fired once through a ground floor window at a toddler who was watching him from inside a house. The toddler was 2 years old. Unra returned home to reload. By then, armed police had begun to converge on River Road. He barricaded himself inside the apartment as officers fired into the walls. A journalist at the Camden Courier Post, Moving on Instinct, found Enra's telephone number in a directory and dialed it. Unra answered. He said he did not know how many he had killed. He had not counted yet, but that it looked like a pretty good score. He said he was too busy to talk. Police threw tear gas canisters through the windows. Unra surrendered, stumbling out of the building into a crowd that shouted abuse and threats at him. A detective frisking him in handcuffs asked whether he was a psycho. Unra replied with calm precision, "I'm no psycho. I have a good mind." He was indicted on 13 counts of first-degree murder. Psychiatric evaluations concluded that he was legally insane. Diagnosed with what the medical language of 1949 called dementia preox, mixed type, with pronounced paranoid coloring. He could not be tried. He was committed indefinitely to the New Jersey State Hospital in Trenton. He would remain there for the rest of his life. His mother was the only person he agreed to receive. She visited him until her death in 1985. Unra outlived her by 24 years, dying in October 2009 at the age of 88. By the end of his life, physicians noted his physical and mental health had deteriorated significantly. He was the oldest person incarcerated in New Jersey at the time of his death. One of his last documented public statements made during a psychological interview shortly before his committ was recorded as follows. I'd have killed a thousand if I'd had bullets enough. The security gate, returned discreetly to the yard by whoever had stolen it on the night of September 5, was found there the following evening. The identity of the person who took it has never been established. Number three, Richard Leonard Kuklinsky. The record begins officially with a body in a 55gallon drum on February 5th, 1980. The body of a 42-year-old man named George Maliband was found in a drum near a chemical plant in Jersey City, New Jersey. He had been shot five times. His tendons had been cut so that the body could be folded to fit inside the container. His brother told police that Maliband had been going to meet Richard Kuklinsky the day he disappeared to complete a transaction for videotape equipment. Maliband had been carrying $27,000. This is where the documented record of Richard Kuklinsk's crimes begins. But Kuklinsky himself would later insist across a long series of prison interviews conducted by investigators, journalists, and criminologists that it was very far from where his crimes actually started. Richard Leonard Kuklinsky was born on April 11th, 1935 in a Jersey City apartment on 4th Street. His father, Stanley, was a Polish immigrant who worked as a railroad breakman and who, by all available accounts, including Kuklinsk's own testimony, was a violent alcoholic who beat his children regularly and sometimes beat their mother. In 1941, Stanley's beatings caused the death of Kuklinsk's 7-year-old older brother, Florian. The parents told authorities the child had fallen down a flight of stairs. No charges were filed. The family buried the truth with the boy. Kuklinsk's mother, Anna, was devoutly Catholic and equally brutal in her own way, using broom handles and household objects as instruments of punishment, sometimes with enough force to break the handle across her son's body. Richard was raised in the Roman Catholic Church and served as an altar boy. He later described his mother as a cancer that destroyed everything she touched and said she and his father together had taught him that violence was the natural language of the household. His younger brother, Joseph, would be convicted in 1970 of raping a 12-year-old girl and murdering her by throwing her from the top of a five-story building. When asked about his brother's crimes, Richard Kuklinsky replied, "We come from the same father." Kuklinsky grew up large. As an adult, he stood 6'4 in and weighed well over 270 lb. He had learned early that his size made most altercations brief, and he had learned to use it without hesitation. By his mid- teens, he was already fighting on the streets of Jersey City with a ferocity that other young men in the neighborhood remembered for the rest of their lives. Kuklinsky would claim in his HBO prison interviews taped in 1992, 2001, and 2003, that he committed his first murder at the age of 14, and that he subsequently killed homeless men as practice. Law enforcement officials have publicly expressed doubt about these specific claims. Investigators who spent years building the case against Kuklinsky, including ATF special agent Dominic Polifron, have said they believed his documented kill count was probably somewhere in the range of 15. The claimed figure of 100 to 200 murders is widely regarded by investigators and criminologists as the product of a man who had learned that the size of the story mattered to the audience. What is not in question is the confirmed record. By the early 1980s, Kuklinsky had built a double life of striking precision. He lived with his wife Barbara and their children in the suburb of Dumont, New Jersey. Barbara described her husband's business to their neighbors as wholesale distribution. She noted he employed an accountant. The Klinskis lived comfortably with large amounts of cash frequently on hand. Cash whose origins Barbara had learned after early and costly experience never to ask about. His criminal network ran through bootleg videotape distribution, pornography trafficking, and stolen goods, and had brought him into contact with associates connected to the Gambino crime family in New York. Through those associations, Kuklinsky had adopted a framework for criminal violence that was defined above all by transaction. Men he believed might inform on him were killed to prevent it. Men who owed him money were killed to demonstrate the cost of default. Men he was asked to kill by others were killed for payment. Between January 1980 and August 1984, Kuklinsky murdered at least five men who have been judicially confirmed. George Maliband shot in Jersey City. Paul Hoffman, a pharmacist beaten to death with a tire iron in a rented garage. His body placed in a drum and left outside a little ferry motel. Gary Smith, a member of Kuklinsk's burglary ring, who had discussed going straight, poisoned with cyanide in a motel room and then strangled when the poison worked too slowly. His body hidden between the mattress and box spring for 4 days, while other guests complained about the smell. Daniel Deppner, another ring member, killed and dumped wrapped in garbage bags beside a remote road in West Milford, New Jersey. Louisie Masque, who had driven to a diner in New Jersey with $95,000 in cash to buy blank videotapes, shot in the head and placed in a freezer, then dumped near a town park 15 months later, still partially frozen on a warm September day, the ice crystals in Maz's body were what gave Kuklinsky his nickname. The medical examiner in Rockland County, New York, where Masay's body was discovered, noted the presence of ice crystals in the tissue on a warm September afternoon. He understood immediately that this was not natural. The body had been stored in a freezer, then disposed of, still not fully thawed, in an attempt to obscure the actual time of death. It was the kind of detail that most killers would not think of or would not have the patience and logistical means to execute. Kuklinsky had both. He had placed Maz in a freezer and left him there for over a year. Law enforcement began connecting the dots through a New Jersey state police officer named Pat Kaine, who had been building a file on Kuklinsky through an investigation into a burglary ring. Kaine and ATF special agent Polyron eventually established a joint task force code named Operation Iceman that dedicated 18 months to building an undercover case. Polyfrron went in as a contact offering contract killings a world Klinsky was comfortable navigating. He recorded conversations. He documented Kuklinsk's willingness to discuss violence, methods, weapons, and fees with the matter-of-fact fluency of someone discussing procurement schedules. On December 17th, 1986, Richard Kuklinsky was arrested outside his home in Dumont, New Jersey. His wife and children had been present moments before. His family, by all accounts, had not known. Barbara Kuklinsky described her husband's two modes, a good Richie and a bad Richie. Good Richie stayed up all night with a sick infant daughter. Bad Richie broke Barbara's nose three times, once tried to run her over with a car, and told her after jabbing her silently from behind with a hunting knife so sharp she did not feel the blade enter that if she tried to leave, he would kill her entire family. Good Richie and Bad Richie were the same man. They always had been. Kuklinsky was convicted of four murders in 1988 and sentenced to four consecutive life terms. In 2003, he received an additional 30-year sentence after confessing in an HBO interview to the 1980 murder of an NYPD detective. He died in Trenton State Prison on March 5th, 2006 at the age of 70. His confirmed body count remains five. The full count may never be determined with certainty. What is established without dispute is that for decades Richard Leonard Kuklinsky drove home to Dumont every evening past the same familiar streets and that his neighbors watched his children play in the yard and that nobody suspected anything at all. Number four, John Emile list. The house on Hillside Avenue in Westfield, New Jersey was lit up for days. every room around the clock. Lights burning through the windows visible from the street day after day while no one moved inside. Neighbors noticed it eventually. The milk wasn't being taken in. The newspapers were piling up. The lights kept burning through the night with the mechanical constancy of a house nobody was living in. A month passed before police entered. They found the family in the ballroom laid out on sleeping bags, arranged as though placed there deliberately and carefully by someone who had taken time to do this correctly. The mother of the house was upstairs in her attic apartment. All five of them had been shot. The killer had left a radio tuned to a religious station, lowered the thermostat to preserve the bodies, removed his own photograph from every family picture in the building, and driven away. John Emil List was not in the house. He had not been there for 30 days. He was gone, so thoroughly and carefully gone that it would take the combined resources of law enforcement, forensic science, and a national television broadcast nearly 18 years to find him. The background of John List is in accumulation, the slow layering of failure, pride, humiliation, and rigid doctrine into something that eventually ran out of structural support. List was born on September 17th, 1925 in Bay City, Michigan. The only child of German-American parents who were first cousins once removed, he grew up devoutly Lutheran with a father who held strict beliefs about the responsibilities of a man to protect and provide for his family. List absorbed those beliefs completely. They became the framework through which he understood his entire life. He served in the army during World War II and later the Korean War. He held degrees in business administration and accounting from the University of Michigan. He rose by the late 1950s to a position as general supervisor of an accounting department. He married Helen in 1951. They had three children. By all outward appearances, John List was the fulfillment of a certain kind of post-war American ideal. The educated veteran, the provider, the faithful Lutheran. What the ideal was concealing by 1965 when the family moved to Westfield, New Jersey, was a financial situation that had been quietly catastrophic for some time. List had accepted a position as vice president of a Jersey City bank. The bank collapsed. He was out of work and had moved his family, including his elderly mother, into a 19 room Victorian mansion called Breeze Null, a property that cost more than he could sustain. His wife Helen was dealing with advancing tertiary syphilis contracted from her first husband and concealed for years, a condition that had combined with alcoholism to leave her by testimony given at trial, paranoid and increasingly unstable. His daughter Patricia, then 16, was involved in the school theater program in ways that List believed were exposing her to sinful influences. His elder son, John Frederick, showed interest in abandoning his faith rather than declare bankruptcy rather than accept what he understood as the public humiliation of failure. List began quietly diverting money from his mother's bank accounts to cover the mortgage. He continued leaving the house every morning dressed for work, driving to the train station in Westfield, sitting on the platform, reading newspapers, and returning home in the evenings as though nothing had changed. He had been unemployed for months before the morning of November 9th, 1971, and no one in his household knew it. On that morning, while his children were still at school, he shot his wife Helen in the back of the head in the kitchen. He shot his mother, Alma, above the left eye in her attic apartment. As his daughter, Patricia, arrived home from school, he shot her. As his son, Frederick, arrived, he shot him. He then drove to the bank to close out his and his mother's accounts. And then to Westfield High School to watch his eldest son, John Frederick, play in a soccer game. He waited. He watched the match. He drove John Frederick home. Then he shot his eldest son multiple times because, as forensic evidence of misfires at the scene demonstrated, John Frederick had tried to fight back. List placed the bodies of his wife and four children on sleeping bags in the ballroom. He cleaned the crime scenes. He lowered the thermostat. He tuned the radio to a religious station. He wrote a five-page letter to his pastor explaining that he had killed his family to save their souls from the corruption of the world. that this was an act of devotion, not of sin, and that he expected God would understand. He removed all photographs of himself from the house. He got in the car and drove away. He had sent notes in advance to the children's schools and part-time employers explaining that the family would be traveling. He had stopped milk and mail and newspaper delivery. The lights, however, left on throughout the house. he had apparently not accounted for. They were the one detail that eventually brought a neighbor to call the police. For nearly 18 years, John List did not exist under the name Robert Clark, the name of a college classmate. He had traveled by train from New Jersey to Michigan, then onward to Denver. He found accounting work. He joined a Lutheran congregation. He ran a church carpool. In 1985, he married a woman he met at a religious gathering. In February 1988, the couple moved to Midlotheian, Virginia, where he resumed work at a small accounting firm and continued attending church, as though the clock had simply been reset in 1971, and nothing had interrupted the life of a reliable church-going accountant. In May 1989, the Fox television program America's Most Wanted broadcast a segment on the Westfield murders and the long fugitive status of their perpetrator. The segment featured a clay bust sculpted by forensic artist Frank Bender that represented what John List might look like at age 63. It bore a remarkable resemblance to the man who was at that moment driving to work in Virginia under the name Bob Clark. A former Denver neighbor saw the broadcast, recognized the description, and contacted authorities. On June 1st, 1989, List was arrested at his Virginia accounting office. He maintained his alias for months. Only after a fingerprint match against his military records, and after evidence found in the crime scene letter was used to confront him directly, did he acknowledge who he was. He was convicted on April 12th, 1990 of five counts of first-degree murder. At sentencing, he said he felt unaccountable for his actions given his mental state. The judge rejected this, stating that John Emile List was without remorse and without honor and sentenced him to five consecutive life terms. List died at a Trenton Medical Center on March 21st, 2008 at the age of 82 of complications from pneumonia. He had spent the last 17 years of his life imprisoned in New Jersey, the same state where the lights in the house on Hillside Avenue had burned for a full month before anyone thought to check inside. The mansion itself, Breeze Null, was destroyed by an arson fire in August 1972, 9 months after the murders. The fire has never been solved. Number five, Bruno Richard Hman in the early spring of 1932. The most famous home in America had a broken window latch. The nursery at Highfields, the Lindberg estate in Hopewell, Hunteran County, New Jersey, should have been the most secure room in the most watched house in the country. Charles Lindberg, the aviator who had become a global celebrity by completing the first solo non-stop transatlantic flight in 1927, was arguably the most recognizable private citizen in the United States. His every move was public property. And yet on the evening of March 4, 1932, someone built a homemade three-section wooden ladder, carried it to the east side of the house, placed it against the exterior wall beneath the second floor nursery window, climbed up, and removed 20-month-old Charles Lindberg Jr. from his crib. They left behind a ransom note demanding $50,000. They left muddy footprints in the soft ground. They left sections of the homemade ladder which broke under the weight of someone climbing down with a child in their arms. And they left what investigators and the public would spend the next 2 and 1/2 years consumed by an absence. Bruno Richard Hopman was not born in New Jersey. He was born on November 26th, 1899 in Commens in the Kingdom of Saxony, a small German town not far from Dresden. He was the youngest of five children. His father died in 1917. That same year, his brother Herman was killed fighting in France. Shortly after, another brother, Max, was killed fighting in Russia. Within months of those losses, Hedman himself was conscripted into the German army. He served in World War I. He survived. He came home to a Germany that was broken, economically destroyed, politically unstable, its social fabric fraying beyond recognition. The postwar years were not kind to young German men with few resources. Halman committed robbery with a pistol, using a ladder to burgle a mayor's residence. He served 3 years in prison, was released, was arrested again on suspicion of further burglaries, and decided that Germany offered him nothing further. He stowed away on an ocean liner, and landed in New York City in November 1923. He was 24 years old and had entered the country illegally. He found work as a carpenter. He settled in the Bronx. He married a German waitress named Anna Schauffeler in 1925. He became a father in 1933. By every measurable standard, his American life by the early 1930s was a quiet one. Skilled labor, modest income, a wife who, by her own later account did not even know his first name was Bruno until he was arrested. The ransom investigation had stretched into years of dead ends and false leads. A go-between named John Condan, a retired teacher who had inserted himself into the case, had twice met the man claiming to be the kidnapper in a Bronx cemetery and had paid him the $50,000 ransom on April 2nd, 1932. The Lindberg baby's body was found on May 12th, 1932 in woods 4 miles from the family home. the child had died from a blow to the head. Many investigators believed the death had been accidental, that the latter had broken during the descent with the baby, and that what had begun as an extortion scheme became something catastrophic in that single moment. The ransom bills became the investigation's pivot. The Federal Reserve and Treasury Department distributed the list of serial numbers. A bank teller in upper Manhattan on September 15th, 1934, recognized a $10 gold certificate deposited by a customer at a nearby gas station as a marked ransom bill. The gas station attendant, suspicious of the certificate, which was by then a rare denomination being withdrawn from circulation, had written the customer's license plate number on the bill's margin. That plate number belonged to a car registered to a German American carpenter in the Bronx named Richard Hedman. Hedman was placed under surveillance, arrested on September 19 after leading police on a brief and unsuccessful effort to evade them through the Bronx streets and taken in for questioning. In his garage, investigators found $14,600 in Lindberg ransom money hidden inside a section of wall. Inside his closet, Condan's address and telephone number had been written on the wood. In one of Hman's notebooks, what appeared to be a handdrawn sketch of a ladder was found. The trial held in Flemington, New Jersey, beginning January 3rd, 1935, was described by contemporary journalists as the trial of the century. Reporters came from around the world. Haman, named the most hated man in the world by one tabloid, sat through it with apparent steadiness, maintaining throughout that the ransom money had been left in his care by a German friend named Isidor Fish, who had since died. The defense argued that the evidence against Hopedman was circumstantial, that no reliable witness had placed him at the crime scene, that his fingerprints were absent from the latter, the ransom notes, and the nursery. The jury convicted him. He was sentenced to death. His appeals failed. New Jerseys governor reviewed the case twice and twice declined to intervene. On April 3rd, 1936, Bruno Richard Hopman was executed by electric chair at Trenton State Prison. Reporters present said he made no statement from the chair. His spiritual adviser recalled that Haman in his cell had said, "I am absolutely innocent of the crimes I am accused of." His wife Anna spent more than 50 years pursuing legal remedies to clear his name, filing suit against the state of New Jersey, former police officers, and the Hurst newspaper chain. The United States Supreme Court declined her requests. She died in 1994. The case remains one of the most consequential criminal convictions in American legal history and one of the most contested. The evidence, while extensive, was also riddled with procedural failures, possible witness contamination, and questions about the chain of custody for the latter wood. What is established without dispute is this. A 20-month-old child was taken from his crib in New Jersey on a March night in 1932 and did not survive. A man was convicted and executed for that crime. Whether the right man was punished for it is a question that American legal history has never fully closed. Number six, Richard Fran Beganwald. He had already killed someone once before, long before the bodies began turning up near the Jersey Shore. In December 1958, 18-year-old Richard Beganwald walked into a grocery store in Bion, New Jersey with an accomplice and shot the owner dead during the robbery. He was caught 2 days later in Maryland after a confrontation with police. He was extradited to New Jersey, convicted of murder, and sentenced to life in prison. He was released on parole in 1975. He had served 17 years. That release on the grounds of good behavior is one of the genuinely unsettling administrative facts embedded in this case. Because what Richard Beganwald's institutional record had not captured, and what the parole board reviewing his case could not have seen from the file was the underlying architecture of the man. His behavior in prison was managed. His behavior in the world was not. Beganwald was born on August 24th, 1940 on Staten Island, New York. His father was a violent alcoholic who beat him regularly. At the age of five, Beganwald set fire to the family home and was sent for observation at a psychiatric facility in Rockland County. At 8, he was drinking and gambling. At 9, he was receiving electroshock therapy at Belleview Hospital in New York. He was placed in the state training school for boys in Warwick, where he spent years being accused of theft and inciting other inmates to escape. At 11, he set himself on fire in his mother's home. At 16, he graduated from the eighth grade. He dropped out of high school within weeks. Every one of these biographical details was part of a record that existed. psychiatric facilities, juvenile institutions, court files. And yet in 1975, the New Jersey parole system concluded that enough time had passed and enough compliance had been demonstrated for the man who walked into a boy grocery store and shot its owner dead at 18 to be placed back into public life. He kept a low profile for 3 years after his release. In 1977, he was suspected of a rape and violated the terms of his parole by failing to report. He was arrested in Brooklyn in 1980 on the rape charge, but released after the victim did not identify him in a lineup. He married and he and his wife moved to Asbury Park, New Jersey, where he struck up a friendship with a man named Darren Fitzgerald. A friendship that would become central to the eventual unraveling of his second career of violence. The known killings in Asbury Park are a matter of forensic record. In November 1981, a woman named Maria Chiella was shot and dismembered. Her body was buried in the basement of Beganwald's mother's house on Staten Island. In April 1982, Deborah Osborne was stabbed to death. Her body was buried on top of Seella's. In September 1982, a prison escape and drug dealer named William Ward was shot multiple times in the head at Beganwald's Asbury Park home and buried in Neptune City. In September 1982, a 17-year-old named Virginia Clayton was abducted. Her body was found 3 days later. In August 1982, 18-year-old Anna Olesovich was found shot four times in the head, fully clothed in a wooded lot behind a Route 35 Burger King in Ocean Township. Olesvich had been walking the Asbury Park boardwalk when Beganwald found her and lured her into his car. She had done nothing to attract his attention. She simply existed in a space that he was moving through. That is precisely what investigators and court records established. That there was no discernable victim profile, no operational logic that a detective could work backward through to the next potential victim. Women who crossed his path were at risk. Men who might compromise his security were at risk. There was no architecture of victimology that could be reverse engineered into a warning. He simply killed people when the impulse moved him to do so. Fitzgerald eventually was the thread that unraveled it. He went to the police after Beganwald showed him the body of another young woman he had hidden in the garage of the Asbury Park house. Police surrounded the property on January 22nd, 1983. They used a ruse to lure Beganwald out of his back door and officers seized him before he could respond. Inside the house, Fitzgerald had retreated to a secret room packed with weapons and refused to emerge until officers threatened to fire through the wall. A search of the property uncovered an arsenal, pipe bombs, a machine gun, handguns, shotguns, illegal drugs, a live puff adder, and its venom collection apparatus, and floor plans for notable area residences and businesses. Fitzgerald became a cooperating witness. He led investigators to the bodies. He described a third victim Beganwald had shown him in the garage. He confirmed the Staten Island basement graves. He described the transportation of bodies, the deliberate burial over earlier victims, the routine indifference with which Beganwald treated the dead. Beganwald was tried and convicted of multiple murders. His death sentence was later overturned and commuted to life imprisonment. He died in Trenton State Prison on March 10th, 2008. The same year, coincidentally, that John List also died. And the same year that Richard Cotttingham was still alive and expanding his confessions, he was 67 years old, and he had spent most of his life either in prison or killing people the moment he was released from it. The parole board that freed him in 1975 after his first murder conviction had looked at the documented record of a man who had been hospitalized for psychiatric treatment at age 5, who had been electroshocked at 9, who had killed a shopkeeper at 18 and determined that 17 years was sufficient. Whether any evidence existed at the time that would have supported a different conclusion is the kind of question that does not get answered easily. What is established is the result. Number seven, Joseph Cinger. The shoe shop was real. The religion was real. The neighborhood in Philadelphia knew Joseph Calinger as a craftsman. A cobbler who had built his business from almost nothing. a man who went to church, who spoke about God, who had a family that he was strict with but present for. What the neighborhood did not know, and what would only emerge piece by piece through the investigative aftermath of January 1975, was that Calinger had been living inside a disintegrating internal world for years, a world in which divine instruction and uncontrollable violent impulse had begun somewhere in the mid 1970s to fuse into one another. Joseph Callinger was born on December 11th, 1935 in Philadelphia as Joseph Lee Brener III. The day after his birth, he was placed into foster care. His father had abandoned his mother and she could not provide for him. On October 15th, 1939, he was formally adopted by an Austrian immigrant couple, Steven and Anna Kallinger, who were unable to have biological children. The adoption would prove to be one of the great documented catastrophes of parenting in the archival record of this case. Steven and Anna Callinger subjected the child to abuse that was by the court record and psychiatric documentation that followed decades later systematic and severe. It included beatings, starvation, being locked in closets, being burned with irons, being forced to kneel on jagged rocks, and being made to consume excrement. When Joseph was nine, he was sexually assaulted by a group of neighborhood boys. The cumulative effect on his psychological development was not subtle, and it did not require retrospective interpretation to identify. It was there in the behavioral record from early childhood onwards. Callinger married twice. His first marriage ended because of domestic violence. His second wife, Elizabeth, had five children with him. He operated the shoe shop. He appeared to the outside world to be managing, to be building something through sheer vocational effort. He was hospitalized repeatedly through the 1960s for psychiatric complaints, including amnesia and suicidal ideiation. In 1972, his children went to police and reported abuse. He was imprisoned. The children recanted. He was released. Two years later, one of his sons, Joseph Jr., was found dead in an abandoned construction site. Callinger had recently taken out a large life insurance policy on his sons. The insurance company refused to pay, suspecting foul play. The death was never conclusively prosecuted, but it marks in retrospect the last legible boundary between what Kinger was and what he was becoming. Beginning in the summer of 1974, Callinger and his 12-year-old son, Michael, began a crime spree that covered Pennsylvania, Baltimore, Maryland, and New Jersey. Their methodology was a particular kind of terrifying in its simplicity. They knocked on doors, represented themselves as salesmen, and waited to be let inside. Once inside, they produced weapons, a pistol, and a knife, and took complete physical control of the family present. They bound them. They forced them to strip. They robbed them. They did this to four families before the fifth visit to a home in Leonia, Bergen County, New Jersey on January 8th, 1975 ended in the death of a 21-year-old nurse named Maria Fashing. Fashing had arrived at the home after the Calingers were already inside and the residents already bound. When Callinger gave an order and she refused to follow it, he stabbed her in the neck and the back. She died from those wounds. One of the stillbound residents managed to get outside the home and call for help. Neighbors responded. Police were called. By the time officers arrived, the Calendars had fled, using a public bus as their getaway vehicle, disposing of weapons and bloodstained clothing along the way. It was an exit so stripped of sophistication that it looked almost surreal against the calculated brutality of what had just occurred inside the house. Pace gathered the abandoned shirt, collected eyewitness accounts, and cross-referenced what they found against Callinger's known history, his domestic violence record, the unresolved death of his son, and a pattern of arson attacks against properties he owned. Father and son were arrested on kidnapping and rape charges. Callinger was eventually charged with three murders. The death of Joseph Jr., the death of a neighborhood boy, and the death of Maria Fashing. He claimed that God had instructed him to kill. Specifically, he told investigators and later testified that a divine voice had commanded him to eliminate the human race. He pleaded insanity. Courtappointed psychiatrists offered divided conclusions. He was ultimately found legally sane and sentenced to life imprisonment on October 14th, 1976. Michael, his son, was judged to have acted under the complete psychological domination of his father. He was sentenced to a reformatory, released at 21, changed his name, and relocated permanently out of state. Callinger made multiple suicide attempts in prison, including trying to set himself on fire. He was transferred between facilities in New Jersey and Pennsylvania. Flora Retta Shriber, the author of Cibil, the landmark work on dissociative identity disorder, spent years interviewing Callinger and wrote a book about his case, The Shoemaker, published in 1983. Callinger died of heart failure on March 26th, 1996 at the State Correctional Institution in Crescent, Pennsylvania. He had spent the last 11 years of his life on suicide watch. The shoe shop in Philadelphia, by then long closed, had become the kind of detail that the neighborhood quietly absorbed and moved past. The man who had built his leatherwork trade by hand. The man who had spoken of God and discipline had spent the final two decades of his life in institutional confinement because he had walked into a house in Leonia, New Jersey, and stabbed a nurse who told him no. Number eight, Anthony Balum. The block on Stent Avenue in Trenton was a block that knew Anthony Balum. Neighbors described him as unassuming, polite, soft-spoken. He had a 10-year relationship with a woman who bore him two children. he kept to himself. He had problems with drugs, crack cocaine primarily, but that was not unusual for the neighborhood, and it was not in itself enough to make him a subject of significant concern. His arrests before 1994 were for drug offenses and burglary. He had the record of a man who made poor choices in a difficult environment. He did not have the record of a man who was planning to murder women. Between October 1994 and July 1996, Anthony Balum strangled and sexually assaulted four women in Trenton, New Jersey. He did it within a 2-m radius of his home. He followed a pattern so consistent that it would in retrospect be unmistakable as method. But the women he chose were not connected to each other, not connected to systems that generated rapid investigative response, and not connected to him by any prior relationship that could surface through standard inquiry. His approach was to cruise the streets in the early hours of the morning looking for women working as sex workers. He would offer crack cocaine in exchange for sex. He would wait until they moved with him to an isolated location, a vacant lot, a run-down building, and then produce a knife, threaten them, rape them, and strangle them. Three of the four women were left in vacant lots. The fourth was left in a derelict hotel. Karen Denise Patterson, 41 years old, was the first documented victim. October 24th, 1994. Valentina Kyler, 29, followed in March 1995. Connie Hayward, 27, followed in April. Then more than a year passed. Then Dborah Anne Walker, 37, was murdered in July 1996. The interval between Hayward and Walker corresponds to a period when Balam had temporarily relocated to Detroit. from July 1995 through January 1996. There are no confirmed murders attributed to him during that period. Investigators later checked with Detroit law enforcement who found no evidence connecting him to any open cases there. The break in the pattern and then the resumption is itself diagnostic. When Balum returned to Trenton in January 1996, he resumed within months. This was not a man who had changed his behavior or who had experienced some corrective event during the Detroit period. He had simply been absent. The case broke when a fifth woman was attacked on February 16th, 1996 and survived. She had been raped and she managed to escape before she could be strangled. At least one other woman had also managed to flee from him during the prior period. These survivors created the documentary record that fixed Balam's face into the investigation. DNA evidence recovered from crime scenes was tested against Balam when investigators zeroed in on him following the discovery of Walker's body in July 1996. The match was confirmed. Two bodies had been found in close proximity to each other. Both raped, both strangled, both placed in locations consistent with his operational range. Neighbors contacted by officers led investigators back to the address on Stasent Avenue. Balam was arrested on August 8th, 1996. He was calm when police brought him in. He spoke to detectives politely, maintaining the manner that his neighbors had always found unremarkable. He admitted to the stranglings. He described the act in terms of rage and power, the sensation of strangling a woman slowly while maintaining complete control over whether she lived or died. He described these feelings with a specificity and directness that investigators present later noted as among the most coldly articulate admissions they had encountered. After a 4-week trial, Anthony Balam was convicted of four counts of murder and four counts of aggravated sexual assault. He was sentenced to life imprisonment with a minimum of 120 years before parole eligibility. By the mathematical projection embedded in his sentence, he will not be considered for parole until August 2116. He remains incarcerated at New Jersey State Prison. He was 31 years old at the time of his arrest. He had lived his entire life within a few miles of the streets where he committed these murders. His neighbors had watched him walk past for years, polite and quiet. Nothing in his bearing that distinguished him from anyone else on that block, and he had, within that same radius of familiar streets, been doing what he was doing. Number nine, Clarence Hill. Duck Island is not an island in any conventional sense. It is a stretch of low, marshy, heavily wooded land along the Delaware River in Hamilton Township, just outside Trenton, New Jersey. remote enough in the late 1930s and early 1940s that couples who wanted privacy from the public eye found it reliable for that purpose. It was a lover's lane. That was its reputation, and that reputation made it for a period of 4 years, one of the most dangerous places in New Jersey. Clarence Hill was born on November 10th, 1910 in Atlanta, Georgia. He had been a Sunday school teacher. He had two children. There is not a great deal documented about the interior of his early life. Certainly nothing that contemporary investigators could have used to connect him to what was happening on Duck Island and in the surrounding area between 1938 and 1942. What is documented is the pattern. On the night of November 8th, 1938, a 20-year-old man named Vincenzo Tanzillo and a 16-year-old named Mary Matovich were parked at Duck Island when a man armed with a 12- gauge shotgun approached their vehicle and demanded money. Tanzilla refused. He was shot dead. Matovich fled from the car. She was shot in the lower body, chased down, and raped. She survived long enough to describe the attack to police, but died from her injuries the following day. Police were initially skeptical of her account, a reaction shaped in part by the fact that Tanzillo was a married man having an affair. The circumstances made the witnesses less sympathetic in the investigative culture of the time, and the case stalled. On October 1st, 1939, a junk collector found a woman's prosthetic leg protruding from a pile of garbage at Duck Island. In a nearby car, he found the body of a 28-year-old mechanic named Frank Casper, shot multiple times in the head and neck. The woman was Catherine Wernern, 36, found not far away, her skull crushed as she had tried to run. Like the first pair, Casper and Verer were conducting an affair. Like the first pair, their unconventional domestic situations delayed and complicated the investigation. The pattern continued into 1940 and 1942, extending into the surrounding townships as couples began avoiding Duck Island itself and sought privacy in other nearby locations. In November 1940, two more people were shot dead in a car in Hamilton Township. In March 1942 near Morrisville, Pennsylvania, a couple was robbed at gunpoint, shot at, and then beaten as they attempted to flee. They survived. They turned in to police a fragment of broken shotgun stock found at the scene. That fragment carried a partial serial number. The serial number was the thread. Investigators traced it through firearms registration records to Hill. He had been drafted into the army in March 1943 and was stationed in South Carolina when he was arrested at his army camp on December 29th, 1943. Hill was tried in 1944. He maintained throughout that his confession had been beaten from him. And the claim was not entirely without complication. Doctors examining the alleged coercion were divided in their conclusions. The jury found him guilty of first-degree murder on December 29th, 1944, exactly 1 year after his arrest. He received a life sentence with the jury recommending mercy. He was a model prisoner. In April 1964, having served 19 years and then been diagnosed with throat cancer, Hill was released on medical parole. Pennsylvania authorities requested his extradition to face crimes he had allegedly committed across the state line, but New Jersey Governor Richard Hughes declined. Hill died of his cancer in Trenton, New Jersey on July 10th, 1973. He was 62 years old. The six confirmed murders at Duck Island and its surroundings. and the two additional attacks in which the victims survived represent a sustained targeting of a specific type of vulnerable encounter. Hill appeared to have selected his victims based on their isolation and their social vulnerability. People engaged in conduct they could not openly report without exposing their private lives to scrutiny. The culture of investigative skepticism that greeted the surviving witness after the first attack in 1938, who died before her account could generate the urgency it deserved, delayed the response at the very moment it mattered most. Duck Island is still there. The Lovers Lane reputation it had in the late 1930s is long gone. The name to people in Trenton today carries a different weight. Number 10. Robert Relen, Burgon County, New Jersey, in October 1975 had a problem that investigators could not yet articulate as a single problem. Between August 1974 and November 1975, eight women had been killed in the northern New Jersey area in a series of homicides that shared certain characteristics. The victims were young. The circumstances pointed to abduction and the manner of death in several cases was consistent with manual or liature strangulation. It was not yet publicly classified as serial homicide. The connection between cases in separate jurisdictions had not yet been formally established. Investigators were working in parallel without a shared framework. In October 1975, the bodies of two young women were found in the Bergen County woods. Susan Haynes and Susan Reev had both been strangled. Both had been abducted in the area prior to their deaths. Both were young, the kind of demographic profile that did not, in the investigative language of the era, automatically trigger the assumption of predation by an organized offender. Robert Redden was already known to Bergen County law enforcement. He was a convicted rapist with a documented pattern of violent sexual offending. He came from a background of relative privilege. His aunt was wealthy and he had over the years alternately cultivated and alienated that family connection. He was charming in the way that a certain category of violent offender frequently is persuasive, composed, superficially engaging. He had been described in prior investigative files as a Ted Bundy-like figure, a man whose apparent social ease made him genuinely difficult to categorize as a threat. On first contact, investigators in Bergen County gathered witness testimony and evidence connecting Redden to the movements of Haynes and Reev before their deaths. A grand jury indictment followed. In January 1977, Realon was formally charged with both murders. Before the murder trial could be fully adjudicated, Realon was convicted of a separate and remarkable charge, conspiracy to murder his own aunt. While awaiting trial on the murder counts, he had plotted from inside a jail facility to arrange the killing of the relative who controlled the family wealth, a plan that was intercepted. In June 1978, he was sentenced to 20 to 25 years on the conspiracy conviction. The murder trials that followed involved a series of retrials, appeals, and procedural challenges that stretched across years. Real was an aggressive and persistent litigant who used the appellet process with sustained dedication. He was ultimately convicted of both murders and received multiple consecutive life sentences. The case of Robert Reelden illuminates a dimension of the criminal justice process that the other cases in this list do not directly present. The extended aftermath of trial and the persistence of institutional challenge. Real continued filing legal motions from prison for decades. As recently as 2025, New Jersey courts were still producing opinions on his parole status. the appellet division upholding the state parole board's denial of release. He was convicted of crimes committed in 1975. He was still challenging the system that confined him half a century later. From inside New Jersey State Prison, Burgon County in October 1975 had a problem that investigators could not yet articulate as a single problem. By the end of the decade, they had a name for it. The name was Reon. And the question of what to do with that name, how long to hold it, how consistently to confine it, how firmly to resist its arguments for release, became a question New Jersey courts have been answering at intervals ever Fence.
fullTextVi: Số một, Richard Francis Codingham. Anh ấy là một người điều hành máy tính. Mỗi sáng anh khoác áo sơ mi có cổ, lái xe đi làm, quản lý cơ sở dữ liệu tại văn phòng Blue Cross Blue Shield ở Tene, New Jersey và về nhà ở những buổi tối đến một ngôi nhà ở ngoại ô nơi vợ và ba đứa con đã sống. Anh ấy đã huấn luyện giải đấu nhỏ. Anh ấy đã tham dự các bữa tiệc sinh nhật ở cơ quan. Ông có một danh tiếng khá dễ chịu trong số các đồng nghiệp, và bắt đầu từ khoảng năm 1967, ông cũng đã giết chết phụ nữ một cách có phương pháp. Khoảng cách giữa hình ảnh và những gì nó che giấu không phải là ngẫu nhiên đối với câu chuyện của Richard Francis Cottingham. Đó là câu chuyện. Bởi vì trong 13 năm xuyên suốt New Jersey và New York, một người đàn ông không có hồ sơ tội phạm, không có sự bất ổn rõ ràng và không có sự gián đoạn rõ ràng nào đối với thói quen sinh hoạt gia đình của anh ta một loạt vụ giết người. được tính toán kỹ lưỡng, được che giấu một cách có phương pháp và rộng rãi đến mức các nhà điều tra thậm chí còn không biết đầy đủ hiểu những gì họ đang giải quyết cho đến sau khi anh ta bị bắt vào năm 1980, và toàn bộ phạm vi những gì Cottingham đã làm sẽ không được biết đến trong bốn khác nhiều thập kỷ sau đó. Cottingham sinh ngày 25 tháng 11 năm 1946 tại Bronx. Gia đình anh chuyển đến Dumont, New Jersey khi anh vẫn còn là một đứa trẻ và sau đó đến River Veil ở Quận Bergen, một thị trấn yên tĩnh phía bắc New Jersey của đường phố sạch sẽ và hàng rào sân sau. Theo lời kể sau này của chính mình, Cottingham đã phát triển sự ám ảnh về sự ràng buộc khi còn là một thiếu niên, một sự chú ý mà ông mô tả không phải là điều gì đó đáng lo ngại mà là một sự mê hoặc. Ông tốt nghiệp trường trung học Pasak Valley ở Hillsdale, New Jersey năm 1964. Kỷ yếu của anh ấy liệt kê anh ấy là thành viên của đội chạy việt dã và điền kinh. Không có gì để đọc trong đó. Sau khi tốt nghiệp, anh bắt đầu làm việc tại phòng thư tín của Công ty Bảo hiểm Nhân thọ Metropolitan ở Manhattan, nơi cha ông giữ chức phó tổng thống. Ông tham gia các khóa học về máy tính, chuyển sang Blue Cross Blue Shield vào năm 1966 và cuối cùng đã trở thành nhà điều hành máy tính lớn. Con đường sự nghiệp đó, tưởng chừng như không có gì nổi bật, đã mang lại cho Cottingham một thứ vô cùng hữu ích, một cú đúp cuộc sống được xây dựng xung quanh thói quen, khả năng dự đoán và vẻ ngoài của sự ổn định. Anh ấy đi làm hàng ngày. Anh ta đã được tính đến. Không ai nhìn qua bề mặt. Ông kết hôn năm 1970 và có ba người con. Đến năm 1978, vợ ông đệ đơn ly hôn với lý do bị bỏ rơi và tàn ác về tinh thần. Bà rút đơn khi ông bị bắt năm 1980, sau đó hoàn tất thủ tục ly hôn sau khi bị kết án vào năm 1981. Những vụ giết người sớm nhất ở Codingham hiện được cho là có liên quan đến năm 1967. Năm đó, Maryanne Delisala, 17 tuổi, biến mất sau khi kết thúc ca làm việc tại một cửa hàng ở Hackinac. Thi thể của cô được tìm thấy 3 tháng sau đó ở sông Payic, bị siết cổ. Cảnh sát kết luận cô đã bị giết ở nơi khác. Vào tháng 10 cùng năm, Nancy Vogel, một bà mẹ hai con 29 tuổi đã kết hôn người mà Cottingham biết, được tìm thấy bị trói trong ô tô của cô ấy ở Ridgefield Park. Cô ấy đã bị bắt 3 ngày trước đó, có vẻ như đang trên đường đi chơi bingo với bạn bè tại một nhà thờ địa phương. Cô ấy đã bị bóp cổ trên một cánh đồng ở Monil. Các nhà điều tra vào thời điểm đó không có lý do gì để kết nối cái chết của một trong hai người phụ nữ với người điều hành máy tính có thái độ ôn hòa ở River Veil. Các vụ giết người là những vụ án riêng biệt ở các khu vực pháp lý riêng biệt. Chúng sẽ vẫn chưa được giải quyết trong nhiều thập kỷ. Đây là đặc điểm nhất quán trong cách thức hoạt động của Cottingham. Anh ta không ủng hộ một địa điểm, một loại nạn nhân hay một phương pháp có thể tạo ra một mẫu có thể nhận biết được.
